title: Al-Ghazali's crisis
hook: a scholar lost his voice and his certainty, left his post, and found his way through Sufi practice

segments.voice: Yesterday, muraqaba: Sufi watchfulness, keeping watch over the heart and knowing you are seen. Your line was watchful. What did you catch moving in you when you stopped? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-eight.

A teacher stands up to lecture, and his tongue won't move. That's how Abu Hamid al-Ghazali tells it, in a short account of his own life called Deliverance from Error. He was teaching in Baghdad, with students in front of him. Then, he writes, his tongue dried up so that he could not teach. Grief took hold of him. He could hardly eat or swallow. The doctors examined him and gave up; the trouble, they said, wasn't in his body. It had settled in his heart. Today is about how he got there, and what he did next.
screen: `A TONGUE THAT WOULD NOT MOVE.` → `THE DOCTORS GAVE UP.` → `IT HAD SETTLED IN HIS HEART.`

segments.voice: The trouble began earlier, in his mind. He writes that he wanted certain knowledge, the kind that leaves no room for doubt. So he tested what he knew. The senses? The eye looks at a shadow and sees it standing still, yet it moves. It looks at a star and sees it as small as a coin, yet reasoning shows it is vast. If reason can correct the senses, he asked, what corrects reason? Perhaps there's a higher judge that would show reason up, the way waking shows up a dream. He fell into a doubt that argument couldn't cure, since every argument is built out of the very things in doubt. And then, he says, he was healed. Not by arranging proofs. By a light that God cast into his breast. Later came the second crisis, the one with the tongue. Now he had answers, but his life didn't match them. Looking honestly at his teaching, he saw how much of it was driven by wanting to be known. He wavered, he writes, between the pull of the world and the call to leave it, until, as he tells it, the choice was made for him, and his tongue stopped. In the end he left Baghdad, gave up his post, and went seeking solitude and the practice of the Sufis. What he found there, he says, couldn't be learned only from books. It had to be tasted. Knowing the definition of health, he writes, is not the same as being healthy. Notice the shape of both crises. He didn't argue his way out of either one. Each time, by his own account, the way through didn't come from a better argument.
screen: `THE SHADOW AND THE STAR.` · `A LIGHT CAST INTO THE BREAST.` · `LEAVING THE POST.` · `TASTED, NOT ONLY KNOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest when you're lost. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one question in your life that won't resolve: a choice, a doubt, something you keep turning over. Don't work on it now. Al-Ghazali couldn't argue his way out, so for these two minutes, don't argue. Set it down beside you, the way you'd set down a heavy bag, and rest. If you pray, you can hand it to God. If you don't, simply leave it there, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Al-Ghazali's crisis. A scholar's doubt, a tongue that would not move, and a way through found by tasting Sufi practice, not by proof. Today's word.

Your line: lost, then found. Today, when something won't come clear, stop pushing for a moment. Step away, a short walk, a glass of water, a pause, before you go back to it. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Al-Ghazali's Deliverance from Error is read as a spiritual autobiography in Islamic thought; Muslims and others turn to it as an account of doubt, of the limits of argument, and of finding a way through Sufi practice.

fork.setup: you're al-Ghazali. you have your answers, but your tongue won't move, and the doctors can't help. what do you do, by his own account?
options: keep lecturing and push through it.
leave the post and seek solitude and the Sufi path.
write a stronger book of proofs.
fork.reveal: he left Baghdad and his post, and went seeking solitude and Sufi practice, where knowledge had to be tasted, not only argued.

original.note: Arabic: taste; al-Ghazali's word for knowing something by experience, not only by description.

trapdoor: what you thought: al-Ghazali's crisis sounds like a scholar losing his faith for good.
what it means: a doubt that argument couldn't cure, a tongue that froze, and a way through found in Sufi practice.
what a scholar hears: Deliverance from Error, where certainty comes by a light cast into the breast, and Sufi knowledge is dhawq, tasting, not definition.

notes: All of Deliverance from Error is paraphrased (Claud Field's 1909 translation exists but is not on the validator list and its wording was not checked). Confirm each beat: the search for certain knowledge; the shadow and the star examples; the dream analogy; the doubt cured 'not by arranging proofs' but by 'a light God cast into the breast'; teaching in Baghdad; recognizing the desire for reputation; wavering between the world and leaving; the tongue drying up, inability to eat, doctors saying the matter was in the heart; leaving his post for solitude and Sufi practice; dhawq (tasting) and the health/definition analogy.
The script gives no dates, ages, number of students or length of travel, under the claims rule. The index hook's 'famous scholar' was softened to 'a scholar'.
Original word: ذَوْق (dhawq), 'taste'; the pronunciation is given as 'DHAWK' (dh as in 'this'). Confirm the term is used in the Munqidh in this sense.
howItsDone: confirm the description of how the book is read is fair.
Editor: hook's repeated 'settled' varied; the teach's closing line now stays with al-Ghazali's own account (no better argument) instead of the narrator's reading that he 'stopped forcing it'.
